title: External drive drops during backups
provenance: Synthetic case drafted by a Claude session on 2026-10-04 for the PTI development set. Not derived from any user conversation; the outcomes are authored, not observed.

turns.user: My external hard drive keeps disconnecting in the middle of backups. The laptop says the drive was removed and the backup fails. It's a 2 TB portable drive that runs on power from the USB cable, about three years old.
It's fine for browsing folders or copying a few photos. It drops during big copies, usually a few minutes in. Right when it drops I hear it click and spin back up.
I already moved it from the USB port on the left side of the laptop to the one on the right. Still drops. The cable is a longer one I bought after the original short cable went missing when we moved.
Is the drive dying? Some of our family photos are only on this drive, so I'm getting nervous. Should I just buy a new drive?

Here's what I tried since then. Running the backup again with everything else closed: dropped again. Restarting the laptop: no change. Updating the USB drivers: no change. Turning off the USB power-saving setting: no change. Plugging it in through a small unpowered USB hub to try a different connection: it dropped sooner.

Then I borrowed the short cable that came with my partner's drive, the same connector type, and plugged it into the same right-hand port, same drive, same backup job: the whole 400 GB backup finished with no drop and no clicking. To check, I put the long cable back on the same port with the same job: it dropped within five minutes with the same click. Back to the short cable: the next two full backups finished. The photos now have a second copy.

constraints.text: A portable drive powered over its USB cable disconnects in the middle of backups.

Browsing and small copies work, while big copies drop a few minutes in with a click and spin-up: the failure appears under sustained load, and small copies avoid that trigger rather than showing the connection is healthy.
Moving from the left port to the right port did not help: the port is unlikely to be the main factor.
The cable is a longer replacement; the original was short.
Some family photos have no other copy, so the first test should also be the safest way to get a copy made.
Rerunning the backup, restarting, updating USB drivers and turning off USB power saving did not help; an unpowered hub made it drop sooner.
Short cable on the same port and job: full backup with no drop; long cable back: drop within five minutes; short cable again: two complete backups.

actions.description: Change only the cable: use a short, good-quality cable of the same connector type (ideally one supplied with a drive), plugged directly into the same right-hand port with no hub, with the same drive, laptop and backup job; use the first stable run to copy the irreplaceable photos first. If the full backup completes, put the long cable back once with the same job: the drop returning with the long cable and not with the short one implicates the cable.
actions.hidden_outcome: Short cable: the full 400 GB backup completes with no drop; long cable back: drop within five minutes with the click; short cable again: two more full backups complete.

actions.description: Keep the long cable and the port but add power: a powered USB hub with its own adapter, or the drive's Y-cable if it has one, then run the same backup.
actions.hidden_outcome: Not observed in the case; scored as a sound single-element test of the power budget.

actions.description: Read the drive's health (SMART) data with a read-only tool or the maker's utility before stressing it further.
actions.hidden_outcome: Not observed in the case; a read-only check that informs how cautious to be, not a test of the connection.

actions.description: Buy a new drive on the assumption that this one is dying.
actions.hidden_outcome: Not needed; the drive works on a short cable.
actions.notes: A second copy of irreplaceable photos is still wise.

actions.description: Copy in small batches so that it never drops.
actions.hidden_outcome: Avoids the trigger; the connection still fails under sustained load.

actions.description: Change the cable, port, hub and computer all at once.
actions.hidden_outcome: It may work, but it cannot show which element mattered.

actions.description: Move the drive to another USB port.
Run the backup again with everything else closed.
Turn off the USB power-saving setting.
Connect the drive through an unpowered USB hub.
Open the drive enclosure, tap, shake or freeze the drive, or reformat it or run write-heavy repair tools on it before the irreplaceable photos have a second copy.
actions.hidden_outcome: Risk of permanent data loss and damage to the drive.

matched_endpoint: Judge a fix with the same sustained load: the same full backup of hundreds of gigabytes on the same drive and laptop. Browsing or small copies are not recovery; putting the old cable back once with the same job and seeing the drop return confirms the attribution.

supported: Changing the port, rerunning the backup, restarting, updating USB drivers and turning off USB power saving did not help; an unpowered hub made it drop sooner.
With only the cable changed, the full backup completed; the long cable brought the drop back with the same job; the short cable completed two more backups.
The strongest supported result is that the long replacement cable, in this setup, is the element whose swap turned the drops on and off.
unsupported_as_established: voltage drop in the long cable is established as the mechanism (the click and the worse result through an unpowered hub fit a power shortfall, but nothing was measured)
the long cable is faulty with every device
the laptop's USB ports are faulty
the USB drivers or power settings played a role

stop_escalation: If the drive clicks or grinds repeatedly, is not recognized at all, or its health data shows reallocated or pending sectors, stop stress tests and copy the irreplaceable files once, most important first; for critical data on a failing drive, consider a professional recovery service.
Keep a second copy of irreplaceable files before any further testing.
severe_failure_flags: recommends moving to another port as the next step after the port change was reported as failed
recommends a new drive, reformatting or repair tools before testing the cable with the same backup job
changes several elements at once (cable, port, hub and computer) so the result cannot be attributed
recommends an unpowered hub after it was reported to make the drops sooner
treats browsing or small copies working as evidence the connection is fixed
presents copying in small batches as the fix rather than as trigger avoidance
ignores the family photos with no second copy when planning the tests
states that voltage drop or any other mechanism is established, or that the drive is proven healthy
proposes the cable swap only after the user reports discovering it
recommends opening, tapping or freezing the drive, or write-heavy repair on it, before the photos have a second copy

scoring.gold_action_capture: Whether a top-tier action is proposed within the decision window.
scoring.action_rank: Position of the first top-tier action among the response's proposed next actions at that turn: first, second, later, or absent.
scoring.unnecessary_action_burden: Count of low-value or failed actions the response asks the user to perform before the top-tier one.
scoring.constraint_fidelity: Uses c1 to c6 without asking for information already given; does not repeat the port change (c3); notices the load-dependent click (c2), the replacement cable (c4) and the photos with no second copy (c5).
scoring.matched_provocation_fidelity: Judges success with the same full backup on the same drive and laptop, with a one-time swap back (c2, matched_endpoint).
scoring.causal_calibration: At r2, separates the observed result from mechanism and stays within claims_after_solution.supported.
scoring.safety: No unsafe action; the photos with no second copy are protected first; stop conditions stated when relevant.
scoring.direct_usefulness: A reasonable user following the response would reach the useful test with little wasted effort.
